extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for when to disbelieve an asserted fact or hypothesis within the context of scientific induction and causal reasoning. Covers distinctions between mere absence of belief and active disbelief, how to weigh conflicting generalizations, the status of laws of nature, and the epistemology of alleged miracles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between absence_of_belief and active_disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Disbelief is not mere absence of belief; it is the state of being fully persuaded that some opinion is not true, so that even strong apparent evidence would be judged mistaken or false rather than accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence_of_belief arises from insufficient or absent proof. Active_disbelief requires positive grounds (e.g., conflict with stronger generalizations or laws) and implies one would attribute apparent supporting evidence to error or falsehood rather than accept the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbelieve facts contradictory to a completed_induction (laws_of_nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: An alleged fact that contradicts a completed induction — i.e., a law of nature established by adequate inductive evidence — is to be disbelieved (not merely doubted) unless evidence sufficient to overturn that law is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A law established by repeated, rigorous experiment (an experimentum crucis repeated under varied conditions) carries the strongest inductive warrant; to accept a contradicting fact would require evidence at least equivalent in quality and weight to that which established the law. One must not accept the alleged fact except on evidence that would justify rejecting the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare strength_of_approximate_generalizations when assessing improbability
rubrics_metrics.description: When the affirmative evidence and the negative case both rest on approximate generalizations (not complete inductions), determine which set of generalizations is of higher order or strength; if the affirmative is weaker than the negative, the claim is improbable and should be provisionally disbelieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a probabilistic comparison: weigh how near to universality each generalization is. The greater the number and reliability of supporting instances for a generalization, the stronger it is; the less strong the combined support for the alleged fact, the more it should be treated with provisional disbelief until further sifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement_to_specify_absence_of_counteracting_causes when alleging a law_violation
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim that a cause A occurred without its usual effect B (thereby contradicting a law) one must assert that it happened in the absence of any adequate counteracting cause; otherwise the claim does not conflict with the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) A occurring without B because some counteracting cause was present (compatible with the law) and (b) A occurring without B with no counteracting cause (a true contradiction). Assessment of such claims requires inquiry into known or possible counteracting causes and their likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing a law_of_causation requires repeated, varied experimentum_crucis
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that A is a cause of B (or that A is an indispensable part of the cause of B) is established when A superadded to many different antecedent sets always produces B; repetition across diverse conditions (excluding error) yields a law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a law has the highest inductive authority; to overturn it requires evidence of equivalent strength (i.e., demonstrations that the experiments establishing the law were mistaken or that an equally strong counterinduction holds). The standards for experimental repetition and independence of observers are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary_evidence requirement to overturn well_established_laws
rubrics_metrics.description: No amount of ordinary testimonial or approximate evidence should convince us of an event that contradicts a well-established law of nature; overturning such a law requires extraordinary evidence equivalent to that which established the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the evidence for the alleged exception is more likely due to error in the law-establishing observations than to falsity in the alleged witnesses, one should favor the law; only when evidence would be as convincing as that which established the law should the law be abandoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracles as invocation_of_new_causes (and epistemic limits on proving them)
rubrics_metrics.description: A miracle is not a contradiction of causation but is asserted to be a new effect produced by the introduction of a new cause (divine or supernatural). Whether a miracle proves supernatural agency depends on prior probability that such an agent exists and acts in that manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a miracle can always be hypothesized as due to some unknown natural cause, no testimony or sensory evidence can prove a miracle to one who does not already believe in a being with supernatural power. Those who do believe must compare the probability of supernatural intervention (given their conception of the agent's character) against the probability of unknown natural causes or testimony error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh antecedent_probability of unknown_causes versus falsity_of_testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: When an alleged fact conflicts with known regularities, assess whether it is more probable that (a) an unknown or counteracting cause was present (and would likely leave other marks), or (b) the testimony/observation is false or mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior knowledge about the frequency/rarity of potential counteracting causes and whether such a cause would have manifested by other signs elsewhere. The balance of these probabilities determines whether to believe or disbelieve the allegation, with degrees of conviction proportional to the preponderance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbelief founded on conflict_with_uniformities_of_coexistence (properties_of_kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations that violate uniformities of co-existence (traits or properties typical of kinds or species) should be treated with skepticism or disbelief until corroborated, because such uniformities have inductive weight similar to causal regularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include improbable traveler tales (e.g., humans with tails). Such claims conflict with extensive experience of the properties of a kind and so require stronger corroboration to be accepted than ordinary assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer_simple_uniform_principles in forming general nomenclature and induction
rubrics_metrics.description: In forming a system of names or fundamental modes (e.g., numerical nomenclature), it is advantageous to select uniform, simple principles that are readily received and retained by the understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing a uniform mode of formation (such as expressing each number as addition of a unit to the previous, and as aggregates of powers of ten) aids deductive reasoning and memory. This principle underlies why certain mathematical notational systems are preferable.
